name: Feature-density histogram of a dictionary
summary: A log-scale histogram counting every feature in one trained autoencoder by how often it fires, which usually splits into an ultralow-density mode the paper discards as a training artifact and a bulk mode it keeps. It is the paper's quick per-run health check, read for its shape and its left edge rather than for any individual feature.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper says plainly that it has no test-loss equivalent for [[dictionary-learning]]: nothing cheap tracks what it wants, which is interpretable features ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]). What it settles for while iterating is [[feature-density]], the fraction of tokens on which a learned [[feature]] takes a nonzero value. It asks two things of every run: how many features came out, and how rare is the rarest one.

Neither survives being averaged. The paper's working hypothesis is that the transformer holds features spread across a whole distribution of densities, the rare ones hardest to reach because they appear so seldom in the data. A mean describes the middle of that distribution and says nothing about its edge; one bar per run keeps the count and loses the edge.

The shape also caught something nobody asked it for. The authors expected each hidden unit to end up either a meaningful feature or completely unused; the histogram showed a third population instead, a spike of units firing on roughly one token in ten million, which no count of [[dead-neurons]] would have flagged, since those units do fire.

The log axis is forced by the numbers: densities run from about $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-2}$, and linearly all five orders of magnitude stack against zero.

### How to read it, step by step

One chart covers one [[dictionary-learning-run]] — a single trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], named in the paper's run notation ([[feature-notation]]). Every hidden unit contributes one count to one bin: a census of a dictionary, not a picture of any feature in it.

The x axis is $\log_{10}$ of density: $-7$ means one token in ten million, $-5$ one in a hundred thousand, $-2$ one in a hundred. Bins are equal width in log space, so a bar spans a fixed ratio of densities, not a fixed difference. The y axis is a raw count of features per bin, not normalised by dictionary width — in an overlay a wider run sits higher for free, so height alone is not the evidence. Units that never fire have density exactly $0$, which has no logarithm; they are absent from the chart, not piled at its left edge.

Look at the left edge first, then hunt for a valley. The narrow spike near $10^{-7}$ is the [[ultralow-density-cluster]]: the paper reports almost none of those features are interpretable and reads them as an artifact of autoencoder training rather than anything in the transformer — [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]. The broad mass to its right is the [[high-density-cluster]], anecdotally almost all interpretable, the name comparative only. Colour differs by figure: single-run charts hand-mark the bars assigned to the ultralow cluster, the grid uses colour for dictionary width.

### What a bad result would look like

For the diagnostic use: one smooth mound, no valley, nowhere to cut, and the count of usable features unreadable. For the sparsity check: a substantial pile of features right of $10^{-2}$, which the paper's own checklist ([[feature-density-diagnostics]]) reads as the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] set too weak.

For the scaling claim: curves growing taller as the dictionary widens while their left edge stays put. That would say the extra capacity is going to duplicates rather than anything new — the signature of having exhausted the model's [[true-features]]. The caption's "suggesting" is an earned hedge: counting features cannot distinguish a genuinely new one from [[feature-splitting]] of an old one.

### Where it comes back

Fig-64 is the clean case, A/16: two modes, a visible gap, the left one labelled. Fig-65 is the same shape for A/5, the widest run at $131{,}072$ units, where the modes run together and the diagnostic stops working; the paper reports that overlap as arriving with large width and a large [[l1-coefficient]], anecdotally and with no threshold, and falls back on [[density-cluster-separation]]. Fig-67 stacks the shape into a grid: five panels of L1 coefficient, six overlaid width curves each, $512$ up to $131{,}072$ ([[expansion-factor]] $1\times$ to $256\times$). Read within a panel for the left edge marching left, across panels for the whole distribution sliding left as the penalty rises. Anyone who learned only "look for two humps" will over-read the two strongest-penalty panels, where the tall spikes are exactly the overlapping case.
